# Independent audit: polyhedral facet speeds already lie in the physical-cone closure

Audited source: \`candidate f454ad16a82f70ca\`.



## 1. Admissibility and fixed integer fibers

Every selected nonvertical constraint has strict slack at a relative interior point of every positive sampled fiber. Finiteness therefore gives uniform persistence of these fiber inballs under a sufficiently small signed coefficient perturbation. The positive spanning margin of the ambient normals is stable and gives a uniform bound on the perturbed polyhedra. Comparing affine constraint errors on that bounded set with the slacks of an ambient interior point gives the asserted order-\(|t|\) homothetic sandwiches.

In this canonical model the projection is exactly \(\operatorname{conv}P\). In fact its facet inequalities occur among the vertical facets: a projection facet contains an \((r-1)\)-dimensional set of bases, and the positive full-dimensional continuous fibers over its lattice vertices give an \((r+d-1)\)-dimensional ambient face. Keeping these vertical constraints fixed already prevents expansion outside the old projection. Alternatively, the source's bounded-neighborhood and finite-lattice-distance argument suffices to exclude new integer bases. The retained own inballs ensure no old sampled fiber disappears. Canonical hull replacement has precisely the old sampled fibers because the perturbed family came from one convex body.

## 2. Sampled-facet ties

At a surface-regular point of a positive fiber, every active nonvertical ambient normal has continuous component pointing along the unique outward fiber normal. Thus its first-order inward constraint is \(v\geq v_i\), and the actual right speed is \(\max_i v_i\). This includes duplicate sampled-facet incidences arising from distinct ambient facets. Fixed vertical constraints impose no continuous speed.

Reversing the coefficient direction gives minus the minimum of the old active speeds, not minus the maximum. The source keeps this distinction and does not claim false stationarity equalities at ties.

## 3. Convex approximation and passage to the separator

For each normal group, \(v_i-Tg_i\) is globally affine in the entire physical point. Its finite maximum with the constant \(-B\) is globally finite and convex. Multiplication by a nonnegative continuous normal cutoff and summation over finitely many groups preserve these properties. The construction works also for the two-point normal sphere in continuous dimension one.

On the old body all gaps \(g_i\) are nonnegative. The approximants are therefore bounded between \(-B\) and \(B\), independently of \(T\). At an old regular boundary point the terms with positive gap disappear and the terms with zero gap retain exactly their affine speeds. The limit is the actual maximum of active speeds. Surface-null lower-dimensional edges cause no difficulty. Dominated convergence applies to the old integrable separator density and separately to every bounded linear energy, volume, and covariance response coefficient.

Consequently the exact signed polyhedral speed inequality is already implied by the old convex-field inequalities. The finite number of continuous normal groups is essential to this explicit cutoff argument; the source makes no unsupported arbitrary-normal limiting assertion.

## 4. What remains outside this audit

The exact inside-support response \(v+[c-v]_+\) contains information omitted by the conservative response \(v\). A closure theorem for its linear physical-speed term cannot reconstruct that nonnegative hinge. The source correctly distinguishes this possible new branch from the already exhausted enlargement of physical velocities. It does not assert that adding inside selectors preserves the desired common separator, nor that approximation transports actual criticality.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
